title: How Woolly Mammoths Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss woolly mammoths: their small Wrangel Island dwarf population, coexistence with humans, the mammoth steppe ecosystem, their insulating coat and circulatory and hemoglobin adaptations, social behavior and long gestation, tusks and teeth replacement, evolutionary origins from African proboscideans, the Pleistocene and the Colombian and steppe mammoth species, theories of extinction (climate change vs. human overkill), de-extinction efforts, and the mastodon comparison. The episode closes with a listener email about Nancy Pearl's rule of fifty for abandoning books and a tour plug.

segments.title: Opening banter and sponsor
segments.summary: Sponsor read for Squarespace, then the hosts introduce the mammoth topic with banter about elephants, the story of the elephant Domini, and the Wrangel Island dwarf mammoths.

segments.title: Mammoths and humans; the Liuba calf
segments.summary: The hosts discuss mammoths living alongside early humans and cave art, the Wrangel Island population surviving until about 4,000 years ago, and the 2007 discovery of the preserved Liuba calf.

segments.title: Mammoth steppe and mammoth diet
segments.summary: The mammoth steppe is described as a rich grassland during the Pleistocene ice ages, where mammoths grazed on grasses and sedges. The hosts note that the ecosystem differed from today's, so modern habitats would not support them.

segments.title: Mammoth coat, fat, and behavior
segments.summary: The mammoth's layered coat, oily skin, and fat are described. Mammoths grazed about twenty hours a day, lived in female-led herds with calves, faced predators like sabretooth tigers and short-faced bears, and had a long 22-month gestation.

segments.title: Tusks, teeth, musth, and lifespan
segments.summary: Tusks are described as modified incisors that curved outward. Mammoths went through six sets of molars over a sixty-year lifespan. Males competed for mates, and the musk gland (musth) is discussed as a pheromone source for establishing mating hierarchy.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Brief break between segments with banter about travel to Paris.

segments.title: Evolutionary origins of mammoths
segments.summary: Mammoths and elephants share a common ancestor in the proboscidean order, which originated in Africa and spread to Eurasia. Early mammoths appeared in Africa millions of years ago, and wooly mammoths adapted to cold as the Pleistocene began. The steppe mammoth is described as the largest, and the wooly mammoth as the smallest.

segments.title: Cold adaptations: circulation and hemoglobin
segments.summary: The hosts describe a countercurrent arrangement of arteries and veins that kept the core warm, and a hemoglobin adapted to release oxygen at low temperatures. Researchers reconstructed this hemoglobin from a 43,000-year-old mammoth by inserting its genes into E. coli.

segments.title: Mammoth extinction theories
segments.summary: The wooly mammoth's North American range and the Colombian mammoth are described. Two extinction theories are discussed: climate change shrinking habitat and food, and human overkill around 12,000 to 13,000 years ago. The hosts favor climate change with human hunting as a contributing factor, and note the lack of strong evidence for mass hunting.

segments.title: De-extinction and mastodons
segments.summary: The hosts discuss two de-extinction approaches using Asian elephants, the ethical questions involved, and the difference between mammoths and mastodons based on teeth. The mastodon's name, its role in the history of extinction science, and Thomas Jefferson's interest are mentioned.

segments.title: Listener mail: Nancy Pearl's rule of fifty
segments.summary: A listener writes about a book discussion, describing Nancy Pearl's rule of fifty for when to abandon a book. A tour date in Boston is also mentioned.
